questions.q: What change does the editorial observe in how people of different faiths speak with one another today?
options: Debate aimed at proving superiority has given way to open discussion with equal respect
Yes. This openness is called a blessing of the age.
Religious meetings are now forbidden
Not quite. The article says: Debate aimed at proving superiority has given way to open discussion with equal respect.
People have lost interest in such questions
Not quite. The article says: Debate aimed at proving superiority has given way to open discussion with equal respect.
Only scholars may now speak on religion
Not quite. The article says: Debate aimed at proving superiority has given way to open discussion with equal respect.
questions.rationale: “The culture of debate has been replaced by discussion. The watchword is that freedom of expression is supreme.”

questions.q: The editorial hopes people may reach the point of saying, “I am right, you may also be right.” What does it say this does NOT mean?
options: That discussion should be avoided
Not quite. The article says: That they end up uncertain – it means going forward with confidence and respect for human dignity.
That they must give up their own beliefs
Not quite. The article says: That they end up uncertain – it means going forward with confidence and respect for human dignity.
That all views are equally mistaken
Not quite. The article says: That they end up uncertain – it means going forward with confidence and respect for human dignity.
That they end up uncertain – it means going forward with confidence and respect for human dignity
Right. Open discussion strengthens conviction.
questions.rationale: “This does not mean that participants in discussion will ultimately emerge from their deliberations in a state of uncertainty.”

questions.q: According to the article, why have so many revolutions replaced one “unwanted system” with another?
options: They were opposed by other nations
Not quite. The article says: Their leaders pursued a society free of all evil, which cannot exist; what they called evil was challenge to be managed.
They lacked enough supporters
Not quite. The article says: Their leaders pursued a society free of all evil, which cannot exist; what they called evil was challenge to be managed.
Their leaders pursued a society free of all evil, which cannot exist; what they called evil was challenge to be managed
Yes. Reaction without regard to realities fails.
They moved too slowly
Not quite. The article says: Their leaders pursued a society free of all evil, which cannot exist; what they called evil was challenge to be managed.
questions.rationale: “All the leaders and reformers were obsessed with an evil-free ideal society, while according to the law of nature the ideal cannot be achieved in this world… ‘evil’ is the wrong name for ‘challenge’.”

questions.q: What does the article advise parents to give their children above material comfort?
options: Freedom from all difficulty
Not quite. The article says: The spirit of hard work, so that they stand on their own feet.
The spirit of hard work, so that they stand on their own feet
Correct. Indulgence removes incentive.
Introductions to influential people
Not quite. The article says: The spirit of hard work, so that they stand on their own feet.
A large inheritance
Not quite. The article says: The spirit of hard work, so that they stand on their own feet.
questions.rationale: “The right way is for the parents to create the spirit of hard work in their children so that they stand on their own feet.”

questions.q: What does the article name as the price of attaining tazkiya (purification)?
options: Giving up whatever stands in its way – bad habits, excess and frivolity
Yes. To gain one thing, another must be let go.
A long journey to a holy place
Not quite. The article says: Giving up whatever stands in its way – bad habits, excess and frivolity.
Years of silence
Not quite. The article says: Giving up whatever stands in its way – bad habits, excess and frivolity.
A payment to a teacher
Not quite. The article says: Giving up whatever stands in its way – bad habits, excess and frivolity.
questions.rationale: “The price for attaining tazkiya is abstaining from everything that goes against achieving this goal.”

questions.q: The Quran promises the patient a reward “without measure.” How does the article describe the path of patience?
options: Avoiding all contact with difficult people
Not quite. The article says: Staying good, moderate and principled even when treated badly or when it costs you.
Returning each act in kind
Not quite. The article says: Staying good, moderate and principled even when treated badly or when it costs you.
Waiting without acting
Not quite. The article says: Staying good, moderate and principled even when treated badly or when it costs you.
Staying good, moderate and principled even when treated badly or when it costs you
Well read. Being good only to those who are good needs no patience.
questions.rationale: “Even when someone is unkind to you, you are good to him. Even if he adopts a provocative stance, you remain moderate in your behaviour.”

questions.article: Ritual Must Arise from the Spirit
questions.q: A man migrated from Makkah to Madinah in order to marry a woman there. What did the Prophet say of his migration?
options: It would not count as migration for the sake of God – an act is judged by its intention
Yes. Form alone has only relative value.
It should be repeated
Not quite. The article says: It would not count as migration for the sake of God – an act is judged by its intention.
It was forbidden
Not quite. The article says: It would not count as migration for the sake of God – an act is judged by its intention.
It was the most praiseworthy of all
Not quite. The article says: It would not count as migration for the sake of God – an act is judged by its intention.
questions.rationale: “Since this individual had migrated for his own private benefit, the migration would not be considered as migration for the sake of God.”

questions.q: The article describes a “merit culture,” a “contacts culture” and a third kind. What marks the third, a divine society?
options: Positions go to the best connected
Not quite. The article says: Each person’s concern is his own purification, with God – not people – as the focus.
No one works for a living
Not quite. The article says: Each person’s concern is his own purification, with God – not people – as the focus.
Everyone holds equal wealth
Not quite. The article says: Each person’s concern is his own purification, with God – not people – as the focus.
Each person’s concern is his own purification, with God – not people – as the focus
Right. Success is measured by the Hereafter.
questions.rationale: “In a divine society, every person’s concern is one’s own purification… In contrast, in a divine society, the focus of people is entirely God.”

questions.q: How does a person of deep faith respond to joy and to difficulty, according to the article?
options: With indifference to both
Not quite. The article says: With gratitude in joy and acceptance in difficulty – both drawing him nearer to God.
With fear in joy and anger in difficulty
Not quite. The article says: With gratitude in joy and acceptance in difficulty – both drawing him nearer to God.
With gratitude in joy and acceptance in difficulty – both drawing him nearer to God
Exactly. Others swing between pride and despair.
With pride in joy and despair in difficulty
Not quite. The article says: With gratitude in joy and acceptance in difficulty – both drawing him nearer to God.
questions.rationale: “If a man of deep faith experiences joy, his heart is filled with gratitude. And if he is faced with a difficulty, he accepts it, regarding it as God’s Will.”

questions.q: What does the chapter Al-Ikhlas (112) say of God, as the commentary summarises it?
options: He is One, depends on none while all depend on Him, and nothing is like Him
Well read. This is the starting point of all Islamic teaching.
He is the first among many
Not quite. The article says: He is One, depends on none while all depend on Him, and nothing is like Him.
He is part of the natural world
Not quite. The article says: He is One, depends on none while all depend on Him, and nothing is like Him.
He is known only to a few
Not quite. The article says: He is One, depends on none while all depend on Him, and nothing is like Him.
questions.rationale: “God is not many. He is only one. All depend upon Him. He depends on none… a unique being Who has no equal.”
